summary: This is a daily-frequency, universally applicable pain with a clearly mapped competitive whitespace: not one of the 11 identified competitors offers an affordable, out-of-the-box cross-platform moderation queue. Every existing solution is either platform-locked (MEE6/Dyno/Carl-bot to Discord, SmokeDetector to Stack Exchange, Automoderator to Reddit), an API-only building block requiring integration work (Hive, Perspective, Copyscape), or enterprise-priced (CleanSpeak at $249/mo, ModSquad custom). The workaround behavior documented — copy-pasting user IDs into spreadsheets, cross-referencing external databases, stitching together scripts and extensions — is the classic signature of an unmet workflow need. Adjacent pricing proof exists ($5–$11.95/mo Discord bot premiums), and the product can be built today by composing mature moderation APIs rather than building ML from scratch. However, the bull case is tempered by the lowest-possible willingness-to-pay (1/5) and economic impact (1/5) scores: the target users are largely volunteers, and free incumbents anchor the price at $0.
strongest_points: Frequency scored 4/5 — moderation queues are a daily, never-finished workflow, and daily-use operational tools have the strongest retention and subscription fundamentals [SRC-0002]

Structural whitespace confirmed by the competitor map: all 11 competitors are platform-native, API-only, or enterprise/service offerings; none delivers a unified cross-platform queue for community moderators, consistent with the low competition score of 2 [SRC-0003]

Documented workaround severity — manual queue review, spreadsheet decision logs, copy-pasted user IDs, external plagiarism searches — shows moderators already invest significant effort in glue work, the strongest behavioral precursor to product adoption [SRC-0001]

Adjacent willingness-to-pay is proven: MEE6 monetizes at $11.95/mo, Dyno and Carl-bot at $5/mo, and CleanSpeak at $249/mo, establishing a pricing ladder from community tier to enterprise that a cross-platform tool can enter at the $10–30/mo mid-point [SRC-0003]

Network-effect and switching-cost potential: a cross-platform user identity/reputation graph improves with every connected community (SmokeDetector's crowdsourced model proves this dynamic works in this exact domain), and once moderation history, rule sets, and sanctions live in one system, churn becomes costly [SRC-0003, SRC-0004]

Timing advantage: mature detection APIs (Hive, Perspective, Copyscape) can be composed as the detection layer, so the product ships as a workflow/queue layer without building ML from scratch — lower capital requirement and faster time-to-market than incumbents faced [SRC-0003]
Global applicability scored 4/5 — spam, abuse, and plagiarism are universal across languages and platforms, so the addressable ceiling is not constrained by geography or niche [SRC-0002]
weaknesses: Willingness to pay scored 1/5 and economic impact 1/5 — the core users (Stack Exchange moderators, most Discord admins) are volunteers without budget authority, and free incumbents (SmokeDetector, native SE tools, Reddit Automoderator) anchor expectations at $0 [SRC-0002, SRC-0003]
Pain intensity 2/5 and urgency 2/5 indicate a chronic annoyance rather than an acute, budget-releasing crisis — the product risks 'nice-to-have' purgatory where users nod but never pay [SRC-0002]

Total platform dependency: the entire value proposition rides on third-party APIs (Discord, Stack Exchange, Reddit) whose access terms, rate limits, and pricing can change unilaterally and destroy the product overnight [SRC-0003]

Thin evidence base: only 4 evidence items underpin the entire case, with no cited customer interviews, spend data, or demand validation — monetization arguments rest on adjacent proxies rather than direct proof [SRC-0001, SRC-0002, SRC-0003, SRC-0004]
